hints: Notice the key condition, ethanolic sodium hydroxide favours elimination to form C=C, not substitution to form an alcohol.
Start with BrCH2CH2CH2CH2Br and remove one HBr from each C-Br end, so two molecules of HBr are lost in total with excess reagent.
Work out the formula of the hydrocarbon left after losing 2 HBr and find its Mr from 12 for C and 1 for H to pick the matching value.
walkthrough:
**Spot the reaction type**

Ethanolic NaOH means dehydrohalogenation, elimination of HBr to make a double bond. Aqueous NaOH would give substitution to an alcohol, but that is not used here.

Rule: $\text{R-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-Br + NaOH (ethanolic)} \rightarrow \text{R-CH=CH}_2 + \text{NaBr + H}_2\text{O}$

**Apply it twice**

We have a dibromoalkane, $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$, and excess reagent until no further reaction. So both Br atoms are removed.

Overall equation:
$$\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br + 2NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_2\text{=CH-CH=CH}_2 + \text{2NaBr + 2H}_2\text{O}$$

**Identify the product and its Mr**

The organic product is buta-1,3-diene, $\text{C}_4\text{H}_6$, with two C=C bonds. This makes sense as the major product after double elimination.

Calculation:
$$M_r = (4 \times 12.0) + (6 \times 1.0) = 48 + 6 = 54$$

options.A: Correct. Double dehydrobromination gives buta-1,3-diene, CH2=CH-CH=CH2. Its Mr is 54, which matches the loss of 2 HBr from 1,4-dibromobutane.
options.B: Incorrect. 56 is the Mr of butene, C4H8. This is the trap of stopping after only one elimination of HBr. With excess ethanolic NaOH, both Br atoms react to give the diene, not the mono-alkene.
options.C: Incorrect. 74 does not fit any sensible double elimination product. It may come from mixing up elimination and partial substitution, for example imagining one Br eliminated and one replaced by OH. Excess ethanolic conditions drive full elimination.
options.D: Incorrect. 90 is the Mr of butane-1,4-diol, HOCH2CH2CH2CH2OH. This is the product with aqueous NaOH by nucleophilic substitution. The question clearly states ethanolic NaOH, so elimination occurs instead.
